# Uplink Data Transmission Method and Device for Reduced Round-Trip Time

## Background and Technical Overview

The present invention relates to an uplink data transmission method and corresponding device that addresses a critical challenge in modern communication systems: the reduction of round-trip time (RTT) during data transmission processes. As communication networks evolve toward increasingly latency-sensitive applications, minimizing user-plane latency has become a paramount concern for network operators and system designers alike. This invention achieves such latency reduction by leveraging transmission conditions characterized by short time slots, thereby enabling faster data exchange cycles between the network side and user equipment (UE), and ultimately contributing to enhanced overall system performance.

## Core Method Description

### Time Slot Determination and Scheduling Signaling

The proposed method begins with the network side performing a critical determination function: identifying an appropriate time slot size suitable for data transmission under the given network conditions. This determination process takes into account various system parameters to establish an optimal time unit that will govern the subsequent transmission scheduling. Once the appropriate time slot size has been established, the network side proceeds to send uplink scheduling signaling to the user equipment. This signaling is generated and transmitted based directly on the previously determined time slot size, ensuring that the UE receives accurate and synchronized instructions regarding when and how to prepare its uplink data transmission.

### Uplink Data Reception According to Scheduled Timing

Following the transmission of scheduling signaling, the network side receives uplink data from the UE according to a predetermined scheduled timing relationship. A key innovation of this invention lies in the definition of the time slot itself: rather than adhering to conventional time unit durations, the time slot is specifically defined as a time unit having a duration smaller than 1 millisecond. This reduction in time slot duration, compared to traditional millisecond-based scheduling frameworks, forms the foundational mechanism through which the invention achieves its RTT reduction objective.

## Scheduling Timing Relationship

The scheduling timing relationship operates according to a precisely defined temporal structure. Specifically, when the network side transmits uplink scheduling signaling during time slot n, the corresponding uplink data from the UE is received by the network side during time slot (n+1), where the value l is selected from a set L of permissible values. This relationship establishes a direct and predictable correspondence between the moment of scheduling signaling transmission and the subsequent moment of uplink data reception, creating a structured yet flexible timing framework.

## Variable Definitions and Flexibility Considerations

Within this timing framework, both variables n and l are defined as integers greater than or equal to zero, ensuring that the scheduling relationship remains mathematically consistent and applicable across sequential time slots throughout the transmission process. The variable L represents the set of selectable values from which l may be drawn, meaning that the offset between the scheduling signaling time slot and the uplink data reception time slot is not fixed at a single value but rather can be chosen from multiple permissible options contained within set L.

This design introduces significant flexibility into the scheduling timing relationship, as it allows the network side to adapt the interval between scheduling signaling and data reception according to varying network conditions, UE capabilities, or other relevant system parameters. Rather than imposing a rigid, one-size-fits-all timing constraint, the invention accommodates a range of scheduling configurations through the selectable set L, thereby enabling the system to optimize performance across diverse operational scenarios while maintaining the overarching goal of reduced round-trip time and minimized user-plane latency.

## Advantages and Technical Benefits

By implementing time slots with durations smaller than the conventional 1 millisecond threshold, combined with the flexible n-to-(n+l) scheduling relationship, this invention offers several technical advantages. First, it substantially shortens the round-trip time required for uplink data transmission cycles, as the reduced time slot duration inherently compresses the temporal distance between scheduling and data reception events. Second, the flexibility afforded by the selectable set L allows network operators to fine-tune the scheduling relationship according to specific deployment scenarios, network loading conditions, or UE processing capabilities, without requiring a complete redesign of the underlying scheduling architecture. Third, the overall reduction in user-plane latency achieved through this method directly translates into improved system responsiveness, which is particularly beneficial for latency-sensitive applications and services that demand rapid data exchange between network infrastructure and end-user devices.

In summary, this invention presents a technically robust and flexible approach to uplink data transmission scheduling that fundamentally reduces round-trip time through the strategic use of sub-millisecond time slots and an adaptable timing relationship, thereby delivering meaningful improvements to overall communication system performance.

# Method and System for Low-Latency Uplink Data Transmission Using Sub-Millisecond Time Slots

## Background

With the evolution of wireless communication systems toward supporting increasingly diverse and demanding applications—such as autonomous driving, industrial automation, remote surgery, augmented/virtual reality, and other mission-critical services—the need for ultra-low latency data transmission has become paramount. Traditional Long-Term Evolution (LTE) and early 5G systems typically employ 1 millisecond (ms) transmission time intervals (TTIs) or subframes as the basic scheduling unit. While this framework has served well for conventional mobile broadband services, it introduces inherent latency constraints that are increasingly incompatible with next-generation use cases requiring round-trip times (RTT) on the order of 1 millisecond or less.

In conventional systems, the process of uplink data transmission typically involves the network transmitting scheduling signaling (e.g., an uplink grant) in one subframe, followed by a fixed and often lengthy waiting period before the user equipment (UE) can transmit corresponding uplink data. This delay stems from the alignment of scheduling and transmission events across multiple full-length subframes, resulting in a cumulative RTT that is unsuitably long for latency-sensitive services. As a result, network operators and standards bodies have sought approaches to shorten these communication cycles without sacrificing overall reliability or spectral efficiency.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention overcomes these limitations by proposing a novel method and system for uplink data transmission that leverages sub-millisecond time slots to significantly reduce user-plane latency in wireless networks. Rather than relying on standard 1 ms TTIs, the invention divides the transmission timeline into shorter time slots—each less than 1 millisecond in duration—enabling faster scheduling and response cycles between the network and the UE.

Specifically, the invention provides a mechanism wherein the network side transmits uplink scheduling signaling to the UE in a given time slot, denoted as slot **n**. According to a predetermined and mutually understood timing relationship between the network and the UE, the UE is configured to prepare and transmit its uplink data in the immediately following time slot, denoted as slot **(n+1)**. The network, correspondingly, is configured to receive the UE's uplink data transmission in slot (n+1) based on this same predetermined timing relationship.

This tightly coupled scheduling-to-transmission timing—compressed into adjacent sub-millisecond slots—effectively shortens the round-trip time required for uplink data delivery. By eliminating the need for the UE to wait multiple full subframes before responding to scheduling signaling, the invention achieves a substantial reduction in latency compared to conventional systems.

## Detailed Description

### System Architecture

In one embodiment, the wireless communication system comprises a network side entity (such as a base station, gNB, eNB, or other radio access network node) and one or more user equipment devices (UEs) capable of communicating over an air interface divided into a series of consecutive time slots. Each time slot has a duration shorter than the conventional 1 ms subframe—for example, 0.5 ms, 0.25 ms, or another sub-millisecond value—depending on the numerology or subcarrier spacing configuration employed by the system.

### Scheduling and Timing Relationship

The network side, upon determining that uplink data transmission is required from a particular UE, generates and transmits scheduling signaling (such as an uplink grant, containing resource allocation information, modulation and coding scheme parameters, and other relevant control information) during time slot n. This scheduling signaling explicitly or implicitly indicates to the UE that the corresponding uplink data transmission is expected in the very next time slot, slot (n+1).

This timing relationship—wherein slot (n+1) immediately follows slot n—is predetermined and known to both the network and the UE, either through static configuration, semi-static signaling, or dynamic indication within the scheduling signaling itself. This predetermined relationship eliminates ambiguity regarding when the UE should transmit and when the network should expect to receive the uplink data, thereby streamlining the communication process.

### Uplink Data Transmission

Upon receiving the scheduling signaling in slot n, the UE processes the scheduling information and prepares its uplink data accordingly. Due to the shortened time slot duration and the immediacy of the response window, the UE is required to perform rapid processing of the received scheduling signaling, including channel estimation, resource mapping, and data encoding, within a significantly compressed timeframe compared to legacy systems. The UE then transmits its uplink data during slot (n+1), in accordance with the resources and parameters specified in the scheduling signaling.

The network side, having transmitted the scheduling signaling in slot n, correspondingly configures its receiver to expect and capture the UE's uplink data transmission during slot (n+1). This synchronized expectation—based on the predetermined timing relationship—ensures that both sides of the communication link are aligned in terms of transmission and reception timing, minimizing any additional signaling overhead that would otherwise be required to negotiate or confirm timing parameters for each transmission cycle.

### Reduction in Round-Trip Time (RTT)

By compressing the interval between scheduling signaling transmission and uplink data reception into a single sub-millisecond time slot transition (from slot n to slot n+1), the invention achieves a marked reduction in the overall RTT associated with uplink data transmission. In conventional systems employing full 1 ms subframes with multi-subframe delays between scheduling and data transmission, the cumulative latency can range from several milliseconds to over ten milliseconds when accounting for processing delays, propagation delays, and retransmission cycles. In contrast, the present invention's approach—utilizing adjacent sub-millisecond slots—can reduce this latency to a fraction of a millisecond, representing a significant improvement in responsiveness.

### Advantages and Applications

This shortened RTT approach offers several key advantages:

1. **Reduced Latency**: By minimizing the time between scheduling signaling and uplink data reception, the invention directly addresses the stringent latency requirements of ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) applications and other time-sensitive use cases.

2. **Improved System Performance**: The reduced latency translates into improved overall system responsiveness, enabling more efficient closed-loop control applications, real-time interactive services, and time-critical industrial applications.

3. **Enhanced Spectral Efficiency**: Because the timing relationship between scheduling and transmission is predetermined, the need for additional signaling exchanges to negotiate transmission timing is reduced, thereby improving spectral efficiency and reducing signaling overhead.

4. **Scalability Across Numerologies**: The invention is adaptable across various sub-millisecond slot durations, allowing network operators to configure the system based on the varying transmission conditions and requirements of different services—ranging from moderate latency reduction needs to the most stringent ultra-low latency scenarios.

5. **Compatibility with Existing Infrastructure**: The invention can be implemented within existing wireless network architectures with modifications primarily focused on the scheduling and timing logic, without necessitating extensive changes to underlying physical layer hardware.

### Conclusion

In summary, the invention provides an innovative and practical solution to the persistent challenge of reducing user-plane latency in wireless communication networks. By employing sub-millisecond time slots and establishing a predetermined timing relationship wherein scheduling signaling in slot n directly precedes uplink data transmission in slot (n+1), the invention achieves a substantially shortened round-trip time. This approach not only reduces latency but also enhances overall system performance, making it particularly well-suited for transmission scenarios that demand short time slots and rapid response cycles, such as those found in URLLC and other next-generation wireless applications.

# Understanding RTT (Round-Trip Time)

Round-Trip Time (RTT) is a fundamental concept in computer networking that measures the time it takes for a signal or data packet to travel from a source to a destination and back again. This metric is crucial for understanding network performance, diagnosing connectivity issues, and optimizing communication protocols.

## What Is RTT?

RTT represents the total time elapsed between sending a request and receiving the corresponding response. When a device sends a packet across a network, the RTT includes:

- The time for the packet to travel to its destination (one-way latency)
- Processing time at the destination
- The time for the response to travel back to the source

This measurement is typically expressed in milliseconds (ms) and provides valuable insight into the overall health and efficiency of a network connection.

## Why RTT Matters

RTT plays a significant role in various aspects of network communication:

**Performance Assessment**: Lower RTT values generally indicate faster, more responsive connections, which is especially important for real-time applications like video conferencing, online gaming, and voice calls.

**Protocol Optimization**: Many networking protocols, including TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), use RTT measurements to calculate timeout values and manage congestion control mechanisms.

**Quality of Service**: Network administrators use RTT data to identify bottlenecks, troubleshoot connectivity problems, and ensure service level agreements are met.

## Factors Affecting RTT

Several elements can influence RTT values:

1. **Physical distance** between communicating devices
2. **Network congestion** along the transmission path
3. **Routing efficiency** and the number of hops data must traverse
4. **Processing delays** at intermediate network devices
5. **Transmission medium** (fiber optic, wireless, satellite, etc.)

## Measuring RTT

Common tools for measuring RTT include the **ping** command, which sends ICMP echo requests and measures the response time. Network professionals also use more sophisticated tools like traceroute to analyze RTT at each hop along a network path, helping identify specific points of latency or failure.

## Conclusion

RTT remains an essential metric in network diagnostics and performance optimization. As applications increasingly demand real-time responsiveness, understanding and minimizing RTT continues to be a priority for network engineers, developers, and service providers striving to deliver seamless digital experiences.

# Patent Abstract and Summary

## ABSTRACT

An uplink data transmission method and apparatus for reducing round-trip time (RTT) in a cellular network are disclosed. The method employs shortened transmission time intervals (sTTIs) having a duration smaller than 1 millisecond, enabling faster scheduling, transmission, and acknowledgment cycles between user equipment (UE) and a base station. A UE receives an uplink grant referencing a shortened time slot structure, transmits uplink data within the reduced-duration slot, and receives corresponding feedback (e.g., HARQ acknowledgment) within a compressed timing window. The shortened slot may be dynamically configured based on subcarrier spacing, service latency requirements, or network conditions, allowing coexistence with legacy 1ms subframe-based transmissions through multiplexing schemes such as frequency-domain partitioning or puncturing. By reducing the processing and propagation delay inherent in conventional 1ms-based scheduling, the disclosed method achieves substantially lower end-to-end latency, making it suitable for ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) applications, including industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and real-time interactive services.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

### Background

Conventional cellular systems, such as those based on Long-Term Evolution (LTE) standards, utilize a fixed subframe duration of 1 millisecond as the basic unit of scheduling and transmission. While sufficient for many applications, this fixed duration imposes a lower bound on achievable round-trip time (RTT), since each uplink transmission, feedback cycle, and retransmission (if required) is constrained by the 1ms granularity. Emerging applications requiring ultra-low latency—such as industrial control systems, autonomous vehicle communication, augmented/virtual reality, and mission-critical services—demand RTT values substantially below what legacy subframe structures can support. There exists a need for a transmission scheme that reduces the fundamental time unit for uplink communication while remaining compatible with existing network infrastructure.

### Summary

The present invention provides a method, apparatus, and system for uplink data transmission utilizing shortened time slots having a duration smaller than 1 millisecond, thereby reducing the round-trip time between a user equipment (UE) and a network base station (e.g., eNB or gNB).

In one embodiment, the method comprises:

1. **Slot Configuration**: The base station configures and signals a shortened transmission time interval (sTTI) structure to the UE, wherein the sTTI duration is a fractional value of the legacy 1ms subframe (e.g., 2, 3, 7, or a symbol-level duration derived from a specified subcarrier spacing).

2. **Uplink Grant Transmission**: The base station transmits a shortened physical downlink control channel (sPDCCH) carrying an uplink grant that references the shortened slot boundaries and indicates timing offsets for data transmission and corresponding HARQ feedback.

3. **Uplink Data Transmission**: The UE transmits uplink data via a shortened physical uplink shared channel (sPUSCH) within the designated shortened slot, using a reduced processing timeline for encoding, modulation, and transmission preparation compared to legacy 1ms-based procedures.

4. **Accelerated Feedback**: The base station transmits HARQ acknowledgment/negative-acknowledgment (ACK/NACK) feedback within a shortened timing window following receipt of the uplink data, enabling faster retransmission decisions when needed.

5. **Coexistence Mechanism**: To ensure backward compatibility, the shortened slots are multiplexed with legacy 1ms transmissions using techniques including but not limited to time-division multiplexing (TDM), frequency-division multiplexing (FDM), or resource puncturing, allowing simultaneous support of both legacy and low-latency UEs within the same carrier.

6. **Dynamic Adaptation**: The shortened slot duration and associated timing parameters may be dynamically adjusted based on factors including UE capability, requested Quality of Service (QoS), traffic type, subcarrier spacing configuration, or network load conditions, optimizing the trade-off between latency and system throughput.

### Advantages

The disclosed method provides several advantages over conventional 1ms-based transmission schemes:

- **Reduced RTT**: By shortening the fundamental transmission unit, the overall round-trip time for uplink data and feedback is substantially decreased, supporting latency-critical applications.
- **Backward Compatibility**: The multiplexing schemes disclosed allow shortened-slot transmissions to coexist with legacy subframe-based transmissions without requiring a complete network overhaul.
- **Flexible Configuration**: The adaptable slot duration allows network operators to balance latency requirements against spectral efficiency and system overhead.
- **Scalability**: The method is applicable across various subcarrier spacing configurations and can be extended to future generations of cellular standards requiring further latency reduction.

### Brief Description of Embodiments

Various embodiments are disclosed, including but not limited to:
- A UE-side method for receiving shortened slot configuration and transmitting uplink data accordingly.
- A base station-side method for scheduling, transmitting grants, and receiving shortened-slot uplink transmissions.
- A system architecture enabling coexistence of shortened and legacy time slots.
- Signaling procedures for indicating sTTI length, timing offsets, and HARQ timing via higher-layer (RRC) or physical-layer (DCI) signaling.

---

An actual patent application would require detailed claims, drawings, and technical specifications developed in consultation with a patent attorney and grounded in specific, novel technical implementation details to satisfy patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, and enablement).*

# Network-Side Method for Low-Latency Uplink Scheduling with Slot n to Slot (n+1) Timing Relationship

## 1. Technical Field

This disclosure relates to wireless communication systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus performed at a network node (e.g., gNB) for scheduling uplink (UL) data transmissions from a User Equipment (UE) with a compressed scheduling timing relationship, wherein an uplink grant transmitted in slot *n* schedules a corresponding physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) transmission in slot *n+1*, thereby minimizing user-plane latency.

---

## 2. Background

In current cellular systems (e.g., NR/5G), the timing relationship between a downlink control channel carrying an uplink grant (PDCCH) and the corresponding scheduled uplink data channel (PUSCH) is governed by a scheduling offset, commonly denoted K2. Legacy and many current deployments use K2 values of 2, 3, 4 or more slots to accommodate:

- UE processing time for decoding the downlink control information (DCI),
- UE capability constraints (e.g., PUSCH preparation time N2),
- Timing advance considerations,
- Network scheduler processing margins.

For latency-sensitive services such as Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC), industrial automation, extended reality (XR), and other time-critical applications, a K2 value of 1 (i.e., grant in slot *n*, PUSCH in slot *n+1*) is highly desirable, but presents scheduling and resource-coordination challenges at the network side. Specifically, the network needs to:

1. Determine UE capability and readiness for K2=1 operation,
2. Perform resource allocation, HARQ management, and power control within a compressed decision window,
3. Coordinate uplink grant transmission with minimal processing delay,
4. Handle contention with other UEs and Layer 1 (L1) measurement/feedback dependencies within the shortened window,
5. Ensure DCI decoding and PUSCH preparation timelines remain feasible for the UE.

This disclosure describes a network-side method and associated architecture enabling reliable and standardized scheduling of UE uplink transmissions using a slot *n* to slot *n+1* (K2=1) timing relationship, while managing the above constraints.

---

## 3. Summary

The disclosed method is executed at a network node and comprises the following high-level operations:

1. **Capability and Context Verification**: The network node verifies, via UE capability signaling and/or configured parameters, that the target UE supports minimum scheduling offset K2=1 (including required subcarrier spacing (SCS), N2 PUSCH preparation time class, and processing capability index).

2. **Configuration of K2=1 Scheduling Set**: The network node configures (via RRC and/or MAC-CE) the UE with a scheduling offset table entry corresponding to K2=1, and activates this configuration when eligible (e.g., via DCI field pointing to the specific row of the PUSCH-TimeDomainResourceAllocation table).

3. **Pre-emptive Resource Reservation and Early Decision Pipeline**: To meet the compressed timing budget, the network scheduler is architected with an early decision pipeline that:
   - Performs channel quality/interference estimation and resource block (RB) allocation decisions ahead of slot *n* boundary using predictive channel state information (CSI) and buffer status reports (BSR),
   - Pre-computes candidate uplink grants for likely UEs before the exact slot *n* scheduling instant, and finalizes/dispatches the grant at the earliest point within slot *n*.

4. **DCI Generation and Transmission in Slot n**: The network node generates the uplink grant DCI (e.g., DCI format 0_1/0_2 or a compressed/low-latency format) within slot *n*, ensuring it is transmitted early enough within the PDCCH monitoring occasion so the UE has maximal available processing time before the PUSCH transmission occasion in slot *n+1*.

5. **Timing Advance and Power Control Anticipation**: Because the compressed K2 window may not allow a full closed-loop update cycle, the network node uses previously acquired or predicted timing advance (TA) and power control parameters (open-loop plus prior closed-loop offsets) to populate the grant, deferring fine correction to a subsequent slot if needed.

6. **HARQ and Retransmission Handling**: The network schedules HARQ feedback and retransmission grants using a HARQ process ID allocation scheme optimized for the reduced round-trip time (RTT) enabled by K2=1, including parallel HARQ process pooling to sustain throughput despite shorter RTT windows.

7. **Fallback Mechanism**: If UE or channel conditions do not support K2=1 in a given instance, the network dynamically falls back to a higher K2 value (e.g., K2=2, 3) as a fallback offset, signaled via DCI, without requiring RRC reconfiguration.

This approach reduces the user-plane one-way and round-trip latency for uplink data by shortening the grant-to-transmission interval from multiple slots to a single slot, while preserving reliability and scheduling flexibility through capability gating and fallback.

---

## 4. Detailed Description

### 4.1 System Architecture

```
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Network Node (gNB)                     │
 │                                                              │
 │  ┌───────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐ │
 │  │ UE Capability  │   │ Early Decision │   │ DCI Generation│ │
 │  │ & Config Mgr   │──▶│ Pipeline (RB/  │──▶│ & PDCCH Tx    │ │
 │  │ (RRC/MAC-CE)   │   │ MCS/TA/Power)  │   │ (slot n)      │ │
 │  └───────────────┘   └────────────────┘   └───────────────┘ │
 │           │                     │                    │       │
 │           ▼                     ▼                    ▼       │
 │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
 │  │      Scheduling Timing Controller (K2 Selector)        │  │
 │  │   - Determines K2=1 eligibility per UE per slot         │  │
 │  │   - Applies fallback K2 if constraints unmet            │  │
 │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                  PUSCH reception window: slot n+1
```

### 4.2 Step-by-Step Method

**Step 1 — UE Capability Acquisition**
The network node receives UE capability information indicating support for minimum applicable K2 value of 1 slot, associated with a specific numerology (SCS) and a PUSCH preparation time capability (e.g., Capability #2 processing timeline per UE processing capability class). The network node stores this per-UE capability record.

**Step 2 — Configuration**
The network node configures, via RRC signaling, a `PUSCH-TimeDomainResourceAllocationList` including at least one row where K2=1. This configuration is UE-specific or bandwidth-part(BWP)-specific. Optionally, a MAC-CE activation/deactivation command enables toggling of the K2=1 mode based on traffic pattern, mobility, or radio conditions, avoiding full RRC reconfiguration overhead for dynamic switching.

**Step 3 — Early Decision Pipeline**
To meet the tightened timing budget of K2=1, the scheduler performs the following ahead of the slot *n* PDCCH transmission deadline:
- **Predictive BSR/CSI Processing**: Uses the most recent BSR and CSI reports (or predicted values via extrapolation/filtering) to pre-select candidate UEs and resource blocks.
- **Pre-allocation of HARQ Process IDs**: Given shortened turnaround, HARQ process IDs are pre-assigned from a pool sized to accommodate the reduced RTT, preventing process ID collision.
- **MCS Selection with Margin**: Since less time is available for last-moment link adaptation updates, the network applies a conservative modulation and coding scheme (MCS) back-off or margin to increase the likelihood of successful first-transmission decoding, compensating for reduced adaptation granularity.

**Step 4 — Grant Finalization and Early PDCCH Transmission**
Within slot *n*, the network node finalizes the resource allocation, MCS, TA command, and power control command and encodes this into the DCI. The DCI is transmitted at the earliest available PDCCH candidate/monitoring occasion within slot *n* to maximize the UE's available decode-and-prepare time before the slot *n+1* PUSCH occasion.

**Step 5 — Timing Advance and Power Control Handling**
- The network node includes the most recently derived TA command in the grant; if a TA update is pending but not yet validated, the node uses the last confirmed TA value and schedules a supplementary TA correction command in a subsequent slot.
- Uplink power control uses a combination of a semi-static open-loop base (derived from path-loss estimate) and the last transmitted closed-loop power control (TPC) command, since a full closed loop update cycle may not fit within the K2=1 window.

**Step 6 — Reception and HARQ Processing**
The network node monitors for PUSCH in slot *n+1* per the granted resource. Upon reception, HARQ ACK/NACK feedback and any retransmission grant follow a similarly compressed timing relationship where feasible, further reducing overall round-trip latency. If retransmission is required, the node may again apply K2=1 scheduling if conditions allow, or fall back to a longer K2 offset.

**Step 7 — Fallback Handling**
If, at the point of DCI generation, the network node determines that K2=1 scheduling is not achievable due to:
- UE capability mismatch for the given BWP/numerology,
- Insufficient processing margin due to control channel congestion,
- TA uncertainty exceeding a threshold requiring closed-loop correction,

then the network node selects an alternate K2 value (e.g., K2=2) from the configured resource allocation table and signals this via the time-domain resource assignment (TDRA) field in the DCI, ensuring uninterrupted scheduling continuity without additional RRC signaling.

### 4.3 Timing Diagram

```
Slot:        n            n+1
             │             │
PDCCH(UL grant)            │
   │─────────┼───▶         │
             │      PUSCH  │
             │   ┌─────────┤
             │   │ UE Tx   │
             │   └─────────┤
             │             │
UE Processing Window: within slot n
(DCI decode + PUSCH prep, N2 timeline)
```

---

## 5. Advantages

1. **Reduced User-Plane Latency**: Cutting the grant-to-transmission gap to a single slot directly reduces one-way and round-trip latency for uplink traffic, benefiting URLLC, XR, and industrial control applications.
2. **Backward Compatibility**: Fallback mechanism to higher K2 values preserves compatibility with UEs or conditions unable to support K2=1, without requiring separate scheduling architectures.
3. **Efficient Resource Utilization**: Early decision pipeline and predictive BSR/CSI processing allow the network to maintain scheduling efficiency despite the compressed timing budget.
4. **Dynamic Adaptability**: MAC-CE based activation/deactivation of the K2=1 configuration allows the network to adapt scheduling latency mode based on real-time traffic and channel conditions without RRC reconfiguration overhead.
5. **HARQ Efficiency**: Pre-allocated HARQ process pooling sustains throughput despite shortened RTT, avoiding stalls due to process ID exhaustion.

---

## 6. Alternative Embodiments

counterfactuals.output:
# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure addresses limitations in conventional wireless communication systems by providing methods, apparatuses, and systems for efficient uplink scheduling signaling utilizing short transmission time intervals and predetermined timing offsets, thereby enabling reduced latency and improved resource utilization in a wireless network.

In one aspect, a method performed by a network node (e.g., a base station, gNB, eNB, or similar network access point) is provided for scheduling uplink transmissions from a wireless device (e.g., a user equipment, UE, or similar terminal). The method comprises transmitting, to the wireless device, uplink scheduling signaling that grants the wireless device access to one or more short time slots for uplink data transmission. As used herein, a "short time slot" refers to a transmission time interval that is shorter in duration than a standard or legacy time slot, thereby facilitating low-latency communication suitable for time-sensitive applications, such as ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) services.

The uplink scheduling signaling further indicates, either explicitly or implicitly, a predetermined timing offset, denoted by a variable l, wherein l is selected from a predetermined set of timing offset values L. The set L may comprise a plurality of discrete offset values, each corresponding to a different candidate timing relationship between receipt of the uplink scheduling signaling and the subsequent uplink transmission by the wireless device. In some embodiments, the value of l may be indicated dynamically within downlink control information (DCI) associated with the uplink scheduling signaling. In other embodiments, the value of l, or the set L itself, may be configured semi-statically via higher-layer signaling, such as radio resource control (RRC) signaling, or may be predefined according to a communication standard or specification.

The predetermined timing offset l defines a temporal relationship between a reference time point—such as the end of the short time slot in which the uplink scheduling signaling is received, or a subframe or symbol boundary associated therewith—and a start of a short time slot allocated for the scheduled uplink transmission. By allowing the timing offset l to be selected from among multiple values in the set L, the network node is afforded flexibility in scheduling uplink transmissions with varying degrees of processing delay, accommodating differences in wireless device capability, traffic priority, propagation conditions, or scheduling constraints, while still preserving a compact and efficient signaling format.

In a related aspect, a method performed by a wireless device is provided, comprising receiving the uplink scheduling signaling from the network node, determining the applicable timing offset l from the set L based on information contained in or associated with the uplink scheduling signaling, and transmitting uplink data in a short time slot determined based on the timing offset l relative to the reference time point.

In some embodiments, the set L is configured such that its constituent offset values are expressed in units of short time slots, symbols, or a combination thereof, allowing for fine-grained control over the scheduling timeline. In further embodiments, the specific value of l applicable to a given scheduling instance may be determined based on one or more factors, including but not limited to: an index of the short time slot in which the uplink scheduling signaling is transmitted, a numerology or subcarrier spacing configuration in use, a processing capability category associated with the wireless device, or explicit signaling included within the uplink scheduling signaling itself.

Corresponding apparatuses are also provided, including a network node comprising processing circuitry and a transceiver configured to perform the network-side method described above, and a wireless device comprising processing circuitry and a transceiver configured to perform the wireless device-side method described above. Additionally, computer program products comprising instructions which, when executed on at least one processor, cause the processor to carry out the methods described herein are provided.

By employing a predetermined set of timing offsets L from which a specific offset l may be selected and signaled in association with uplink scheduling within short time slots, the embodiments disclosed herein enable a network to flexibly balance latency, signaling overhead, and wireless device processing time requirements, thereby improving overall system efficiency and supporting a wide range of use cases with differing latency and reliability requirements.

# PATENT APPLICATION

## TITLE OF THE INVENTION
**METHOD AND APPARATUS FOR REDUCING ROUND-TRIP TIME IN 5G/LTE COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS USING SUB-MILLISECOND TIME SLOT SCHEDULING FOR UPLINK TRANSMISSION**

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

[0001] The present invention relates generally to wireless communication systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for reducing round-trip time (RTT) latency in Fifth Generation (5G) New Radio (NR) and Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks through the use of sub-millisecond time slot structures for scheduling and executing uplink (UL) transmissions between a network node and a user equipment (UE).

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0002] Modern wireless communication systems, including LTE and 5G NR, are increasingly required to support latency-sensitive applications such as autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, augmented/virtual reality, and remote surgery. These applications demand round-trip times on the order of 1 millisecond or less.

[0003] Conventional LTE systems utilize a Transmission Time Interval (TTI) of 1 millisecond, which inherently limits the minimum achievable RTT due to the time required for scheduling requests, grant allocation, data transmission, and acknowledgment procedures. Even with 5G NR's introduction of flexible numerology and mini-slot scheduling, existing scheduling architectures often fail to fully exploit sub-millisecond granularity for uplink transmissions, particularly with respect to the scheduling request (SR) and uplink grant procedures that precede actual data transmission.

[0004] Existing uplink scheduling procedures typically involve: (a) a UE transmitting a scheduling request on a Physical Uplink Control Channel (PUCCH); (b) the network processing the request and transmitting an uplink grant via Downlink Control Information (DCI); and (c) the UE subsequently transmitting data based on the received grant. This multi-step process introduces cumulative latency that is particularly pronounced when each step is bound to slot durations of 1 ms or longer.

[0005] There exists a need in the art for improved methods and apparatus that reduce the end-to-end RTT for uplink transmissions by restructuring the time-domain scheduling grid into sub-millisecond units, while maintaining compatibility with existing frame structures, and enabling faster grant-to-transmission cycles between the network and the UE.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0006] The present invention addresses the foregoing needs by providing a method and apparatus for reducing RTT in 5G/LTE systems through the definition, signaling, and utilization of sub-millisecond time slots ("mini-slots" or "micro-slots") specifically optimized for uplink scheduling request, grant, and transmission procedures.

[0007] In one embodiment, a method is provided, performed at a network node (e.g., a gNB or eNB), comprising: dividing a standard 1 ms subframe into a plurality of sub-millisecond time slots, each having a duration less than 1 millisecond; configuring a UE with a sub-slot-based scheduling request resource; receiving, from the UE, an uplink scheduling request within one of the sub-millisecond time slots; generating an uplink grant within a subsequent sub-millisecond time slot occurring within the same 1 ms subframe or within a time interval shorter than a legacy TTI; and transmitting the uplink grant to the UE such that the UE may commence uplink data transmission within a reduced number of sub-millisecond time slots relative to conventional slot-based scheduling.

[0008] In another embodiment, a method is provided, performed at a UE, comprising: receiving configuration information defining a plurality of sub-millisecond time slots within a subframe; transmitting a scheduling request during a designated sub-millisecond time slot; monitoring a control channel for an uplink grant during a subsequent sub-millisecond time slot; and transmitting uplink data during a sub-millisecond time slot identified by the received grant, thereby reducing the round-trip time associated with the scheduling-request-to-transmission cycle.

[0009] In a further embodiment, an apparatus is disclosed comprising a processor, a transceiver, and a memory storing instructions that, when executed, cause the apparatus to perform the sub-millisecond scheduling operations described herein.

[0010] Additional embodiments include dynamic adjustment of sub-slot duration based on channel conditions, UE capability signaling for sub-slot support, and hybrid scheduling wherein certain UEs operate under legacy 1 ms scheduling while others operate under the sub-millisecond scheme within the same cell.

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

[0011] **FIG. 1** illustrates a wireless communication system comprising a network node and a plurality of UEs configured to operate according to sub-millisecond time slot scheduling, in accordance with an embodiment of the invention.

[0012] **FIG. 2** illustrates a subframe structure divided into a plurality of sub-millisecond time slots for uplink scheduling request and grant procedures.

[0013] **FIG. 3** is a signaling flow diagram illustrating the exchange of scheduling request, uplink grant, and uplink data transmission messages between a UE and a network node using sub-millisecond time slots.

[0014] **FIG. 4** is a flowchart illustrating a method performed by a network node for reducing RTT using sub-millisecond scheduling.

[0015] **FIG. 5** is a flowchart illustrating a method performed by a UE for reducing RTT using sub-millisecond scheduling.

[0016] **FIG. 6** is a block diagram of an exemplary network node apparatus configured to perform the disclosed methods.

[0017] **FIG. 7** is a block diagram of an exemplary UE apparatus configured to perform the disclosed methods.

[0018] **FIG. 8** illustrates a comparative timing diagram showing RTT reduction achieved by the sub-millisecond scheduling scheme relative to conventional 1 ms TTI-based scheduling.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### System Overview

[0019] Referring to FIG. 1, a wireless communication system 100 is shown comprising a network node 110 (which may be an eNB in an LTE deployment, a gNB in a 5G NR deployment, or a hybrid node supporting both) and one or more UEs 120a-120n. The network node 110 and UEs 120 communicate over an air interface 130 configured according to a frame structure that includes a plurality of subframes, each subframe further divided into sub-millisecond time slots as described in greater detail below.

[0020] It will be understood that the terms "sub-millisecond time slot," "mini-slot," and "micro-slot" are used interchangeably herein to refer to a scheduling and transmission unit having a duration shorter than the conventional 1 ms subframe/TTI used in legacy LTE systems.

### Sub-Millisecond Slot Structure

[0021] Referring to FIG. 2, a subframe 200 of duration 1 ms is illustrated as being partitioned into N sub-millisecond time slots 210a-210n, where N is an integer greater than one. In an exemplary embodiment, N is selected such that each sub-slot 210 has a duration in the range of approximately 0.0625 ms to 0.5 ms, corresponding to subcarrier spacing configurations consistent with 5G NR numerology (e.g., 15 kHz, 30 kHz, 60 kHz, or 120 kHz), though the invention is not limited to these specific values.

[0022] Each sub-millisecond time slot 210 comprises a control region 212 and a data region 214. The control region 212 is configured to carry scheduling-request resources, uplink grant (DCI) information, or both, depending on whether the sub-slot is designated for network-to-UE or UE-to-network signaling. The data region 214 is configured to carry the physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) transmission or downlink control/data as applicable.

[0023] In an embodiment, the network node 110 configures, via radio resource control (RRC) signaling, downlink control information (DCI), or a combination thereof, a set of sub-millisecond time slots reserved for expedited scheduling-request and grant exchange, distinct from sub-slots used for regular data scheduling.

### Method Performed at the Network Node

[0024] Referring to FIG. 4, a method 400 performed by network node 110 is described.

[0025] **Step 402:** The network node divides a subframe into a plurality of sub-millisecond time slots, each having a duration shorter than a legacy 1 ms TTI. This division may be performed based on a selected numerology, cell configuration, or UE capability information received during initial access or RRC connection setup.

[0026] **Step 404:** The network node transmits, to a UE, configuration information identifying the sub-millisecond time slot structure, including the location and periodicity of scheduling-request resources and the mapping of sub-slots to uplink grant opportunities.

[0027] **Step 406:** The network node monitors a designated control resource within a given sub-millisecond time slot for receipt of a scheduling request from the UE.

[0028] **Step 408:** Upon receiving the scheduling request, the network node generates an uplink grant within a time interval measured from receipt of the request that is shorter than the legacy grant-processing interval associated with 1 ms TTI scheduling. In an embodiment, this interval is less than or equal to one sub-millisecond time slot duration.

[0029] **Step 410:** The network node transmits the uplink grant to the UE within a subsequent sub-millisecond time slot occurring within the same subframe as the received scheduling request, or, in an alternative embodiment, within an immediately following sub-millisecond time slot irrespective of subframe boundary.

[0030] **Step 412:** The network node monitors for and receives an uplink data transmission from the UE within a sub-millisecond time slot identified by the transmitted grant.

[0031] In an optional embodiment, Step 408 further comprises dynamically adjusting a processing delay parameter (K2 or equivalent) based on measured UE processing capability, reported via a UE capability information element, such that grant-to-transmission timing is minimized on a per-UE basis.

### Method Performed at the UE

[0032] Referring to FIG. 5, a method 500 performed by UE 120 is described.

[0033] **Step 502:** The UE receives, from the network node, configuration information defining a sub-millisecond time slot structure and associated scheduling-request resources.

[0034] **Step 504:** Upon determination that uplink data is available for transmission, the UE transmits a scheduling request during a next available sub-millisecond time slot designated for scheduling-request signaling.

[0035] **Step 506:** The UE monitors a physical downlink control channel resource within a sub-millisecond time slot subsequent to the transmitted scheduling request for receipt of an uplink grant.

[0036] **Step 508:** Upon receiving the uplink grant, the UE determines a designated sub-millisecond time slot for uplink data transmission, as indicated within the grant, and prepares uplink data accordingly.

[0037] **Step 510:** The UE transmits uplink data during the designated sub-millisecond time slot, wherein the elapsed time between generation of uplink data and successful transmission is reduced relative to legacy 1 ms TTI-based scheduling procedures.
